blocks.md: In a competitive labor market a firm can hire as many workers as it wants at the going wage. A monopsonist is a firm big enough in its local labor market that, to hire more, it must raise the wage, and it must pay that higher wage to everyone it already employs, not just the new hire. Each extra worker therefore costs more than their own wage. The firm responds by hiring fewer people and paying less than a competitive market would. A minimum wage changes that calculation: once the wage is fixed by law, hiring one more worker no longer raises the pay of the others, so the firm hires more. Set at the right level, a minimum wage can raise both wages and employment.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is the main theoretical reason a minimum wage need not cost jobs, and it underlies tests that compare minimum-wage effects in more and less concentrated labor markets.
A firm with revenue $p\,q(L)$ faces inverse labor supply $w(L)$ with $w'(L) > 0$. Profit is $\pi(L) = p\,q(L) - L\,w(L)$, and the first-order condition is

blocks.tex: \underbrace{p\,q'(L)}_{\text{marginal revenue product}} = \underbrace{w(L) + L\,w'(L)}_{\text{marginal cost of labor}}

blocks.md: Because $w'(L) > 0$, the marginal cost of labor exceeds the wage, so the monopsonist hires $L_{mon}$ below the competitive $L_{eff}$ and pays $w_{mon} = w(L_{mon})$, below the competitive wage.
With a binding minimum wage $w_{mw}$, the marginal cost of labor is flat at $w_{mw}$ until the supply curve is reached. Employment is
So employment is hump-shaped in the minimum wage, peaking at $w^*_{mw} = w_{eff}$. A "well-chosen" minimum wage lies between $w_{mon}$ and that upper wage.

blocks.md: With $w(L) = 4 + L/50$ and MRP $= 20 - L/50$: competitive employment solves $4 + L/50 = 20 - L/50$, so $L_{eff} = 400$, $w_{eff} = 12$. The monopsonist sets MC $= 4 + 2L/50$ equal to MRP: $L_{mon} = 266.7$, $w_{mon} = 9.33$ (while MRP there is 14.67). A minimum wage of 11 raises employment to $50(11 - 4) = 350$; 12 gives the maximum, 400; 14 gives $50(20 - 14) = 300$; above 14.67 employment falls below the monopsony level. blocks.md: Labor-market concentration is a common proxy: the [Herfindahl-Hirschman Index](note:herfindahl-hirschman-index) of employers' shares of hiring or vacancies in an occupation and area. Where concentration is high, minimum-wage employment effects should be less negative, or positive.

- **Thinking any minimum wage helps under monopsony.** Above the competitive wage it lowers employment, just as in a competitive market.
- **Using the supply curve as the cost of labor.** The monopsonist's relevant cost is the marginal cost curve, which lies above supply.
- **Equating monopsony with a single employer.** Any upward-sloping supply to the firm (search frictions, commuting costs, job differentiation) gives some wage-setting power.
